title: Author's purpose
subject: READING
subtopic: Analyze Point of View, Purpose, Features, and Structure

slides.title: Why did the author write it?
slides.text: Every author has a **reason** for writing. We call it the **author's purpose**.

slides.title: Three big reasons
slides.text:
To **inform**: to teach you facts.
To **persuade**: to make you think or do something.
To **entertain**: to tell a fun story.

slides.title: How to tell
slides.text:
1. Does it give **facts**? Inform.
2. Does it say **you should**? Persuade.
3. Is it a **fun story**? Entertain.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Find the words that show the purpose.

Facts and numbers show **inform**.
**Should**, **must** or **best** show **persuade**.

Point to them.

sentences.t: They eat leaves from tall trees.
Their necks can be two meters long.

example.explain: These sentences give **facts** about giraffes. There is no story and no **you should**. The author wants to **inform** us.

together.passage: You should eat fruit every day. Fruit is sweet and good for you. It helps you grow strong. Ask for fruit at lunch!
together.stem: Why did the author write this?
options: To tell a funny story
To get you to eat fruit
To tell how fruit grows
To describe a lunch box
together.hint: Look for the words You should. What does the author want you to do?
together.good: Yes! You should and Ask for fruit show the author wants you to eat fruit.

sentences: You should eat fruit every day.
Fruit is sweet and good for you.
evidence.stem: The answer was: to get you to eat fruit. Tap a sentence that tells you what to do.
evidence.wrong: This sentence gives a reason. Find a sentence that tells you to do something.

checks.passage: The sun is a star. It is very hot. It gives Earth light and heat.
checks.stem: Why did the author write this?
options: To teach facts about the sun
To make you laugh
To get you to go outside
To tell a story
checks.why: The text gives facts about the sun, so the author wants to inform.

checks.passage: A little goat wanted to fly. He climbed a hill and flapped his ears. He did not fly, but he rolled all the way down, laughing!
checks.stem: Why did the author write this?
options: To teach facts about goats
To get you to climb a hill
To tell a fun story
To show how to fly
checks.why: A goat that tries to fly is a fun, made-up story to entertain.

checks.passage: Our school needs a bigger playground. There is no space to run. Please help us ask for a new one!
checks.stem: Why did the author write this?
options: To tell a story about a playground
To teach facts about schools
To describe a game children play
To get readers to help ask for a bigger playground
checks.why: The author says the school needs a bigger playground and asks readers to help.

again.title: Ask the author
again.text:
Pretend you can ask the author: **Why did you write this?**

Would they say: "to teach you", "to change your mind" or "to make you smile"?
again.example:
Text: Brush your teeth two times a day. It keeps them strong.

The author would say: **to get you to brush your teeth.** That is persuade.

slides.title: General and specific purpose
slides.text:
The **general purpose** is the big reason: inform, persuade or entertain.

The **specific purpose** is the exact reason: **to explain how bees make honey** or **to describe life on a pearling boat**.

slides.title: Informational texts
slides.text: Most informational texts aim **to inform**. Their specific purpose may be to **explain** how or why, to **describe** something, to **compare** two things, or to give **instructions**.

slides.title: Find the specific purpose
slides.text:
1. Find the topic.
2. Ask: what does the author **do** with it? Explain, describe, compare, tell how?
3. Put them together: **to explain how volcanoes form**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Check the **whole** text.

1. What do most sentences do? Give steps? Give reasons? Describe?
2. The specific purpose must cover the **whole** text, not one sentence.
3. Point to sentences that show it.

sentences.t: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through raindrops.
Each drop bends the light and splits it into colors.
That is why rainbows often appear just after rain, when the sun comes out.

example.explain: General purpose: **to inform**. Every sentence explains **how** or **why** rainbows form. Specific purpose: **to explain how rainbows form**.

together.passage: Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches. A mother turtle crawls out of the sea at night and digs a hole with her back flippers. She lays about a hundred eggs, covers them with sand and returns to the water. About two months later, the baby turtles hatch and race toward the sea.
together.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To persuade people to visit beaches
To tell a funny story about a turtle
To compare turtles and fish
To explain how sea turtles lay eggs and hatch
together.hint: Does the author tell you to do something or tell a story? What do most of the sentences explain?
together.good: Yes! The sentences explain, step by step, how turtles lay eggs and how babies hatch.

sentences: Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches.
A mother turtle crawls out of the sea at night and digs a hole with her back flippers.
She lays about a hundred eggs, covers them with sand and returns to the water.
About two months later, the baby turtles hatch and race toward the sea.
evidence.stem: The answer was: to explain how sea turtles lay eggs and hatch. Tap 2 sentences that show this.
evidence.wrong: This sentence introduces the topic. Find sentences that explain the steps.

checks.passage: The Arabian leopard is one of the rarest big cats in the world. It has pale gold fur with dark spots. It lives in rocky mountains and hunts at night. Only a small number survive in the wild today.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To persuade people to buy a cat
To describe the Arabian leopard
To tell a story about a hunt
To explain how mountains form
checks.why: Every sentence describes the leopard: its fur, home, habits and numbers.

checks.passage: Both wolves and pet dogs belong to the same family of animals. Wolves live in the wild in packs, but dogs live with people. Wolves hunt for their food, while dogs are fed by their owners.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To compare wolves and dogs
To warn people about wolves
To explain how to train a dog
To tell a story about a wolf
checks.why: The text shows how wolves and dogs are alike and different. Its purpose is to compare.

checks.passage: To fold a paper boat, first fold a sheet of paper in half. Then fold the top corners down to the middle. Next, fold the bottom edges up on both sides. Finally, open the middle and press it flat into a boat.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To describe the history of boats
To persuade you to buy paper
To tell how to fold a paper boat
To compare boats and ships
checks.why: The text gives steps in order: first, then, next, finally. It tells how to fold a paper boat.

again.title: Verb + topic
again.text:
A specific purpose is a **verb + topic**.

Verbs: **explain**, **describe**, **compare**, **tell how**, **persuade**.

Pick the verb that matches what most sentences do.
again.example:
Text: Steps for planting a seed.

Verb: **tell how**. Topic: **plant a seed**. Purpose: **to tell how to plant a seed**.

slides.title: Purpose in true stories
slides.text: **Literary nonfiction**, like a memoir or biography, tells a true story. Its purpose may be to **share an experience**, to **show what a person was like**, or to **teach a lesson** learned from real life.

slides.title: Purpose in persuasive texts
slides.text:
A **persuasive** text has a specific goal: to make readers **believe** something or **do** something.

The specific purpose names that exact goal: **to convince the town to build a library**.

slides.title: Steps
slides.text:
1. Decide the general purpose.
2. Ask: what exact message or action does the author want?
3. Look for strong clues: the opening, the ending, and repeated ideas.
4. Choose the answer that fits the **whole** passage.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Authors often state their purpose in the **opening** or **closing** sentences.

1. Read them closely.
2. Check that the middle sentences support that purpose.
3. Reject purposes that fit only one part.

sentences.t: I used to think my grandfather's stories were boring.
Then one summer, he told me how he crossed the desert by camel as a boy.
I began writing down every story he told.
Now I know that the people around us carry history we can learn from, if we only listen.

example.explain: This is a true story (memoir). The last sentence shows the lesson. Specific purpose: **to share how the writer learned to value the stories of older people**.

together.passage: Every afternoon, students at our school throw away dozens of plastic water bottles. Most are used only once. If each student brought a refillable bottle, we could cut this waste almost completely. Refillable bottles are cheap, and there are already water fountains on every floor. I am asking the student council to start a Bring Your Bottle campaign next month, and I hope every class will join.
together.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To explain how plastic bottles are made
To describe the water fountains in the school
To convince students to use refillable bottles and join a campaign
To tell a story about the student council
together.hint: Look at the last sentence. What exactly does the author ask for?
together.good: Yes! The author gives reasons and then asks for a Bring Your Bottle campaign.

sentences: Every afternoon, students at our school throw away dozens of plastic water bottles.
If each student brought a refillable bottle, we could cut this waste almost completely.
Refillable bottles are cheap, and there are already water fountains on every floor.
I am asking the student council to start a Bring Your Bottle campaign next month, and I hope every class will join.
evidence.stem: The answer was: to convince students to use refillable bottles and join a campaign. Tap 2 sentences that show what the author wants.
evidence.wrong: This sentence describes the problem or gives a fact. Find sentences that say what the author wants people to do.

checks.passage: When I was nine, I was afraid of water. My father took me to the sea every Friday. At first I only sat on the sand. Week by week, I stepped further in. By the end of the summer, I was swimming beside him. I learned that fear gets smaller when you face it one small step at a time.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To teach readers how to swim
To persuade readers to visit the sea every Friday
To describe the beach on Fridays
To share how the writer overcame a fear step by step
checks.why: The memoir tells a true experience and ends with the lesson: face fear one small step at a time.

checks.passage: Our town should open a public library. Right now, the nearest one is an hour away. A library would give students a quiet place to study and give families free books. It could also host classes for adults. The town council should vote yes next week.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To describe the libraries in other towns
To convince the council to vote for a library
To explain how libraries lend books
To share a memory of reading
checks.why: The author gives reasons and ends by asking the council to vote yes.

checks.passage: One young scientist spent ten years studying mangrove forests on the Gulf coast. She waded through mud at dawn to count young trees and measure the water. Her careful records helped show which areas were shrinking. Her life's work reminds us that protecting nature often begins with patient observation.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To show how one person's patient work helps protect nature
To explain how to measure water
To persuade readers to become scientists when they grow up
To list the plants that live in mud
checks.why: The passage describes one scientist's patient work and ends with the message that protecting nature begins with observation.

again.title: Listen to the ending
again.text:
In memoirs and persuasive texts, the **ending** often tells you the purpose.

It may give the **lesson** learned, or the **action** the author wants.
again.example:
Ending: "So next time you see litter, pick it up."

Action: **pick up litter**. Purpose: **to persuade readers to pick up litter**.

slides.title: Precise purposes
slides.text:
Strong readers name purpose **precisely**. Not just "to inform" but **to correct a common misunderstanding about deserts**, or **to honor a teacher by showing her influence**.

Authors may also have **more than one** purpose.

slides.title: Purpose of a part
slides.text:
Every part of a text has a job. An anecdote may **hook** the reader. A statistic may show a problem is **serious**. A counterargument may show the author is **fair** before answering it.

Ask: why did the author put **this** here?

slides.title: Analyze purpose
slides.text:
1. Identify the main purpose of the whole text.
2. Notice the author's choices: tone, examples, what is included or left out.
3. For a part, ask how it serves the main purpose.
4. Reject purposes that are too general or that only fit a detail.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Prove a precise purpose with **the author's choices**.

1. Point to the opening and the closing.
2. Point to words that show tone (admiring, warning, correcting).
3. Show how the middle supports the purpose you named.

sentences.t: Many people picture deserts as empty, lifeless places.
Yet after a rare rain, seeds that waited for years can sprout and bloom within days.
Beetles collect water from fog, and foxes hunt in the cool hours of the night.
The desert is not empty; it is full of life that knows how to wait.

example.explain: The opening states a **common belief**, and the ending **corrects** it. The middle gives proof. The precise purpose: **to correct the mistaken idea that deserts are lifeless**.

together.passage: My grandmother never went to school. She could not read a newspaper, but she could read the sky, telling us when a dust storm was coming hours before the radio did. She knew which desert plants could soothe a cough and which could make you ill. She ran a household of nine children, kept accounts of every coin in her head and settled arguments between neighbors with a single proverb. When people today say someone is uneducated, I think of her. There are many kinds of knowledge, and some of the deepest are never written in books.
together.stem: What is the author's specific purpose in this passage?
options: To honor the grandmother and show that knowledge comes in many forms
To explain how to predict a dust storm
To argue that schools are not useful
To list the plants that grow in the desert
together.hint: Read the last two sentences. What point do the grandmother's skills prove?
together.good: Yes! The author honors the grandmother and uses her skills to show there are many kinds of knowledge.

sentences: My grandmother never went to school.
She could not read a newspaper, but she could read the sky, telling us when a dust storm was coming hours before the radio did.
She knew which desert plants could soothe a cough and which could make you ill.
She ran a household of nine children, kept accounts of every coin in her head and settled arguments between neighbors with a single proverb.
When people today say someone is uneducated, I think of her.
There are many kinds of knowledge, and some of the deepest are never written in books.
evidence.stem: The answer was: to honor her and show that knowledge comes in many forms. Tap 2 sentences that state this purpose.
evidence.wrong: This sentence gives an example of her skills. Find the sentences where the author states the bigger point.

checks.passage: Some argue that video calls make travel for meetings unnecessary. It is true that calls save time and money. However, studies of teams show that people who meet in person build trust faster and solve conflicts more easily. Companies should keep calls for routine updates, but still bring teams together for important decisions.
checks.stem: Why does the author include the sentence It is true that calls save time and money?
options: To prove that traveling to meetings is always better
To change the topic to money
To show fairness by admitting a point before answering it
To explain how video calls work
checks.why: The author admits a strength of the other side, then answers it with However. This makes the argument seem fair.

checks.passage: The night the power failed across the city, the street outside our building turned dark and silent. Then a neighbor carried out a lamp, another brought tea, and children who had never spoken began to play together. By morning the lights were back, but something had changed. We still greet each other by name.
checks.stem: What is the author's specific purpose?
options: To explain why power failures happen in large cities
To warn readers to buy lamps
To describe the neighbors' homes
To show how a shared difficulty brought neighbors closer
checks.why: The story moves from silence to sharing, and ends showing the neighbors still greet each other: the hardship brought them together.

checks.passage: In 1960, a small country produced almost no fresh water of its own. Today, it supplies most of its drinking water from desalination and recycles much of its wastewater for farms. This change did not happen by chance. It took decades of planning, investment and public campaigns to save water.
checks.stem: What is the purpose of the final two sentences?
options: To give the exact cost of desalination
To explain that the change came from deliberate effort
To describe how wastewater is cleaned
To suggest the change was lucky
checks.why: They tell readers the change came from planning, investment and campaigns, not by chance.

again.title: The author's job title
again.text:
Give the author a **job title** for this text.

Teacher? Lawyer arguing a case? Storyteller? Someone giving thanks? Someone correcting a mistake?

The job title points to the precise purpose.
again.example:
Text: praises a grandmother's skills and says knowledge is not only in books.

Job title: **someone giving honor and correcting a narrow idea**. Purpose: **to honor her and show many kinds of knowledge**.
